takeaways.title: Diverse Renewable Technologies are Key to Emission Reductions.
takeaways.description: Solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal, and hydrogen are playing a crucial role in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and accelerating the global energy transition. Each technology has unique advantages, such as solar PV’s affordability, wind energy’s scalability, hydropower’s grid stability, geothermal’s reliability, and hydrogen’s potential for hard-to-abate sectors.

takeaways.title: Implementation Challenges Must Be Addressed.
takeaways.description: While renewable energy technologies offer significant benefits, their implementation faces challenges, including high initial investment costs, grid integration issues, financing constraints, and infrastructure limitations, particularly in developing countries.

takeaways.title: Strategic Approaches are Essential for Scaling Renewable Energy.
takeaways.description: Policy incentives, innovative financing (e.g., blended finance and concessional loans), infrastructure development (grid modernization and energy storage), capacity building, and community engagement are key strategies for scaling up renewable energy deployment, ensuring equitable access, and supporting a just energy transition.

concepts.title: energy and air quality
concepts.body: Energy and air quality refer to the relationship between energy production and consumption and the impact it has on the cleanliness and health of the air we breathe, including pollutants released from energy sources.

concepts.title: land use planning
concepts.body: Land use planning is the process of evaluating and designating how land in a specific area should be used, balancing development needs with environmental protection and community interests.

concepts.title: lifecycle ghg emissions
concepts.body: Lifecycle GHG emissions refer to the total greenhouse gas emissions associated with a product or service throughout its entire lifecycle, including extraction of raw materials, production, transportation, use, and disposal.

content.text: Case Example: Market-Based Mechanisms: The India "PAT" Model

India’s Perform, Achieve, and Trade (PAT) scheme is one of the most successful examples of a market-based energy efficiency 💬️ program designed specifically for a developing country context.
The PAT scheme identifies "Designated Consumers" (DCs) in energy-intensive sectors like thermal power, steel, cement, and textiles. Instead of a flat tax, it uses a cap-and-trade approach:
Target Setting: Each DC is given a specific target to reduce its "Specific Energy Consumption" (energy used per unit of production) based on its current level of efficiency. This ensures that plants that are already efficient are not unfairly penalized.
Certification: Plants that exceed their targets are awarded Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts).
Trading: Plants that fail to meet their targets must buy ESCerts from more efficient plants to comply with the law.
In its first cycle, the PAT scheme achieved an energy reduction of 5.3%, surpassing its initial target and demonstrating that market mechanisms can drive efficiency without stifling industrial growth.

5: Industrial Symbiosis and Circularity
Industrial Symbiosis is a collaborative approach where the waste or byproduct of one industry becomes the raw material for another. This is often facilitated by Eco-Industrial Parks (EIPs), which provide the geographical proximity needed for the physical exchange of heat, water, and materials.

Renewable Process Heat
For low and medium-temperature heat, technologies like industrial heat pumps and solar thermal systems are now mature and cost-effective.
For example, Brazil's PotencializEE has supported over 400 SMEs, including ice cream manufacturers, in installing heat pumps to replace inefficient gas boilers, leading to energy cost reductions of up to 47%.

3: Green Public Procurement (GPP)
Governments are among the largest buyers of cement, concrete, and steel for infrastructure. By prioritizing the purchase of "green" materials, governments can create a guaranteed market that reduces the risk for companies to invest in low-carbon production.
Effective GPP policies use Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs), standardized "nutrition labels" for the carbon footprint of materials, to help procurement officers make informed choices without needing deep engineering knowledge.

4. Technology Leapfrogging and New Paradigms
Developing countries have the unique advantage of being "latecomers," allowing them to bypass the polluting stages of industrial development that wealthier nations went through.

Green Hydrogen
In sectors like steel and fertilizers where carbon is part of the chemical process, green hydrogen is a transformative solution. Transitioning to Hydrogen-based Direct Reduced Iron (H2-DRI) can eliminate up to 90% of a steel mill's direct emissions. For instance, with its vast geothermal and wind resources, Kenya is exploring the use of green hydrogen to produce domestic fertilizers. This would not only reduce emissions but also improve food security and reduce the national trade deficit caused by importing fossil-fuel-based ammonia.

Digitalization and Real-Time Monitoring
The "Fourth Industrial Revolution" offers digital tools that allow managers to track energy use minute-by-minute. Real-time monitoring can flag machinery running outside of production hours or detect air leaks in compressed gas systems, common but costly issues that can save 10% to 30% in energy costs with minimal investment.

1: Energy Efficiency and Management Systems

Energy efficiency is often called the "fifth fuel" because it is the fastest, cheapest, and lowest-risk way to reduce energy costs and emissions. For an individual enterprise, improving efficiency can strengthen the bottom line by reducing direct energy costs by 10% to 30%.
Industrial Energy Management Systems (EnMS)
The most powerful tool for sustained efficiency is the implementation of an Energy Management System, such as the ISO 50001 standard. Unlike a one-time equipment upgrade, an EnMS is a framework that makes energy efficiency a core part of a company’s management culture. It involves setting achievable targets, creating action plans, and constantly measuring progress.

Policy makers can support EnMS by:
Mandating Energy Managers: Requiring large industrial facilities to appoint a designated energy manager and file annual consumption reports.
Subsidizing Audits: Providing grants for SMEs to conduct professional energy audits, which are "medical check-ups" for a factory’s energy health.
System Optimization Training: Moving beyond individual components (like a more efficient motor) to "system optimization" (ensuring the entire pumping or steam system is designed correctly). Optimization often yields savings far greater than just replacing individual parts.

The complexity of the industrial sector means that no single policy can achieve <ai prompt="Clarify decarbonization.">decarbonization 💬️</ai>. Instead, policy makers must deploy a "policy package" that addresses efficiency, technology, market demand, and finance simultaneously. This section details the most effective strategies grounded in the experience of developing nations.

content.title: B: Key innovations for Decarbonizing the Sector

content.text:
Capacity and Infrastructure Constraints

The transition to clean industry requires a supportive ecosystem that is often lacking in emerging economies. Grid bottlenecks are a common problem; a factory may want to install electric boilers or rooftop solar, but the local grid may not be able to handle the variable input or the increased demand.

There is also a significant "capacity gap", a lack of skilled people to manage the change. Many countries lack a sufficient number of certified energy auditors, managers, and engineers who know how to identify energy-saving opportunities or maintain advanced clean energy systems. Without this human infrastructure, even well-funded projects can fail due to poor implementation or maintenance.

Capacity and Infrastructure Constraints

The transition to clean industry requires a supportive ecosystem that is often lacking in emerging economies. Grid bottlenecks are a common problem; a factory may want to install electric boilers or rooftop solar, but the local grid may not be able to handle the variable input or the increased demand.

There is also a significant "capacity gap", a lack of skilled people to manage the change. Many countries lack a sufficient number of certified energy auditors, managers, and engineers who know how to identify energy-saving opportunities or maintain advanced clean energy systems. Without this human infrastructure, even well-funded projects can fail due to poor implementation or maintenance.

Economic and Financing Barriers
The economics of heavy industry are notoriously challenging. Steel, cement, and bulk chemicals are undifferentiated commodities, meaning buyers focus almost entirely on price. These industries typically operate with low profit margins and high capital intensity. This leaves very little room in corporate budgets for "risky" investments in unproven low-carbon technologies.

Moreover, the "green premium", the additional cost of producing a low-carbon product compared to a traditional one, can be substantial. Without policy intervention, a steel mill that invests in green hydrogen will likely be undercut by a competitor using cheaper, high-emitting coal. This leads to "carbon leakage," where production simply shifts to regions with weaker environmental regulations rather than emissions being reduced globally.

Financing is also a major hurdle. In developing countries like Indonesia and Vietnam, the gap between the finance available and the amount needed for a just energy transition 💬️ is estimated at 70% to 90%. Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs), which form the backbone of many industrial supply chains, face even greater difficulties. They often lack the financial capacity to fund decarbonization or the technical expertise to prepare "bankable" projects that can attract international investors.

While the opportunity for industrial transformation is clear, the barriers to achieving it in the real-world context of developing countries are formidable. These challenges are technical, economic, and institutional in nature, and they often interact to stall progress.

Why Industry is Critical for Climate Action

The industrial sector is often described as "hard-to-abate" because of its reliance on high-temperature heat and its inherent process emissions. However, it is precisely because of these challenges that the sector is critical for climate action, particularly in developing countries.

First, industry provides the materials necessary for the green transition itself. The massive infrastructure needed for a low-carbon economy, wind turbines, solar panels, and upgraded electricity grids, will be built primarily from steel, cement, and aluminum. If these materials are produced using today’s carbon-intensive methods, the "carbon debt" created by building green infrastructure could undermine global climate goals.

Second, the industrial sector in developing countries represents a unique opportunity for "leapfrogging". Because much of the industrial infrastructure in these nations is still being built, policy makers have the chance to integrate high-efficiency, low-carbon technologies from the outset. It is far less expensive to build an efficient factory from scratch than it is to retrofit an old one, as is common in developed economies. Failing to act now results in a "permanent loss" of mitigation potential that will persist for decades until those facilities are eventually replaced.

Energy-Related vs. Process-Related Emissions

A crucial distinction for policy makers, and one often overlooked in non-technical discussions, is the difference between energy-related emissions and process-related emissions.

Energy-related emissions result from burning fossil fuels to provide the heat or power needed for industrial work. For example, when a boiler burns natural gas to create steam, or a furnace burns coal to melt metal, the resulting CO2 is an energy-related emission.These emissions can be reduced by improving the efficiency of the boiler or by switching from coal to a cleaner fuel like electricity or biomass 💬️.
Process-related emissions, however, are released not from burning fuel, but as a direct byproduct of the chemical reactions required to transform materials into a new product. These are "inherent" to the chemistry of production and are among the most difficult emissions to abate. Notable examples include:

Cement Production: In the "calcination" step, limestone (calcium carbonate) is heated to produce clinker. This chemical reaction releases CO2 as a byproduct regardless of how the kiln is heated.
Steelmaking: In a traditional blast furnace, carbon in the form of coke is used to strip oxygen away from iron ore. This chemical reduction process inherently produces.
Chemicals: The production of ammonia for fertilizer or certain industrial gases often results in the release of nitrous oxide or CO2 as part of the molecular transformation.

The Mechanism of Industrial Emissions

To design effective policies, it is necessary to understand how industry generates greenhouse gases. These emissions are broadly categorized into three "scopes," which help organizations and governments track where and how carbon is released.
Direct emissions (Scope 1) are produced at the industrial facility itself. These occur through the on-site combustion of fossil fuels for power or heat, chemical reactions in the production process, and "fugitive" leaks from equipment like refrigeration or gas pipelines.
Indirect emissions (Scope 2) are associated with the energy the facility purchases, most commonly electricity. While the emissions happen at a distant power plant, they are attributed to the industrial user because the factory’s demand drove the generation of that power.
Value chain emissions (Scope 3) are the most complex, covering all indirect emissions that occur in the upstream production of raw materials or the downstream use and disposal of the products sold. For many manufacturers, Scope 3 emissions can be the largest part of their total carbon footprint, representing the "embodied carbon" in their supply chains.

The industrial sector is a central pillar of the global climate challenge. It is responsible for more than one-third of global primary energy use and an equivalent share of energy-related carbon dioxide emissions. In rapidly industrializing nations like India, the sector accounts for nearly 30% of greenhouse gas emissions and is projected to become the largest single source of national emissions by 2040 as other sectors, such as transport and power, decarbonize more quickly.

content.title: B: Industry, Energy, and Climate Change

content.text:
Regional Energy Dynamics and Growth

The geography of industrial energy consumption is undergoing a historic shift toward the developing world. Projections indicate that between 2012 and 2040, industrial energy demand in non-OECD countries will grow at an average rate of 1.5% per year, compared to just 0.5% in OECD countries. By 2040, it is expected that non-OECD countries will account for nearly 73% of the world's total industrial energy consumption.
This growth is driven by the urgent need for infrastructure, roads, bridges, power plants, and housing, all of which are made from energy-intensive steel and cement.Policy makers in these regions face the "lock-in" effect: industrial facilities like blast furnaces or cement kilns require massive capital investments and can remain in operation for 40 to 50 years. Decisions made today regarding the energy systems of new factories will dictate a country’s emission trajectory and energy security for the next half-century.

The data indicates that industrial energy use is more concentrated in developing regions like ASEAN, often with a higher reliance on coal compared to the more diversified and electricity-heavy mix found in developed regions like the EU. For the policy maker, this underscores the dual challenge of reducing the carbon intensity of industrial fuels while managing the rapid growth in total demand.

The Role of Feedstocks

A unique characteristic of industrial energy use that policy makers must grasp is the concept of energy feedstocks. In many industrial processes, fossil fuels are not burned to create heat; instead, they are used as raw materials that become part of the final product.1 Natural gas is the primary feedstock for agricultural chemicals and nitrogen-based fertilizers, while petroleum products like naphtha are essential for manufacturing plastics.1 This "non-combustion" use of energy is a significant portion of the total industrial footprint and presents a distinct challenge for decarbonization, as it requires finding entirely different chemical building blocks rather than simply switching to a cleaner fuel source.9

Cement Production

Cement manufacturing is a major industrial emitter, responsible for approximately 8% of the world's total CO2 emissions. In 2022, global cement manufacturing produced 1.6 billion metric tonnes of CO2. Unlike many other sectors where energy combustion is the primary source, more than half of the emissions from cement and concrete production are "process emissions". These direct emissions largely result from the calcination of calcium carbonate (limestone), which breaks down to yield lime and CO2. The combustion of fossil fuels for high-temperature processing units accounts for another 30-40% of emissions, while electricity usage for transport and operations contributes indirectly.

Steel Production

The steel industry is also highly energy- and carbon-intensive, accounting for approximately 7-11% of total global CO2 emissions. Most CO2 emissions from iron and steel manufacturing result from the reduction of iron ore in blast furnaces (BFs), which use coke (a form of coal) in an energy- and carbon-intensive process. The weighted average carbon footprint of steel is estimated at 1.85 tons of CO2 per tonne of steel produced, though this can vary significantly based on production method.

The Classification of Industrial Activity

To manage industrial energy effectively, policy makers must first understand how the sector is organized. Industrial energy use is typically categorized into three distinct groupings based on the nature of the activity and its energy intensity: energy-intensive manufacturing, non-energy-intensive manufacturing, and non-manufacturing.

1: Energy-intensive manufacturing

Energy-intensive manufacturing is dominated by five primary sub-sectors: iron and steel, chemicals and petrochemicals, non-metallic minerals (primarily cement and glass), non-ferrous metals (primarily aluminum), and pulp and paper. These industries are characterized by their reliance on massive amounts of thermal energy and electricity to transform raw materials. For instance, the production of steel from iron ore requires immense heat for melting and shaping, while the chemical industry consumes energy both for heat and as a physical ingredient, or feedstock, for products like fertilizers and plastics.

The industrial energy end-use sector encompasses a diverse and complex array of activities, ranging from the extraction of raw materials to the manufacturing of finished goods. It is the largest consumer of delivered energy globally, accounting for approximately 54% of total delivered energy consumption. In the context of developing nations, this share is often even more pronounced, frequently exceeding 50% of the total energy supply, excluding transport. This high concentration of demand creates a persistent tension between the goals of rapid economic growth and the constraints of an often-unreliable or expensive energy supply.

content.title: A: Understanding the Industrial Energy End-Use Sector

content.text: Lesson 1 Overview

The industrial sector is a major contributor to global CO2 emissions, responsible for about a quarter of energy-related emissions. Most of this comes from fossil fuel use, particularly coal. Industrial emissions have risen by 70% since 2000, driven by growing global demand for goods. While emissions stabilized during the COVID-19 pandemic, they rebounded in 2021. A 2% decline in 2022 was due mainly to reduced activity in China's industrial sector and the global energy crisis. However, emissions in other regions continued to rise, and global industrial emissions are likely to grow under a baseline scenario.
